gist: Ed Yardeni grades new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a middling 'five,' forecasts an actual September rate HIKE (not a cut) as the Fed belatedly fights above-target PCED inflation, flags Treasury Secretary Bessent's yen intervention and bond-buyback moves as unimpressive but revealing of bond-market vulnerability, and reiterates his 'Roaring 2020s' bull case built on an AI-driven productivity boom, an S&P 500 year-end target of 8,400, and a $5,000 year-end gold target.

themes.theme: Fed Chair Warsh's Hawkish Pivot and a Contrarian September Hike Call

insights.claim: Ed Yardeni grades Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a middling 'five out of ten' — not terrible, not great — because Warsh repeated his generic 'price stability' commitment for a second straight press conference despite core inflation having run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A Fed chair still 'punting' on decisive action despite years of above-target inflation signals continued policy inertia risk that investors should not assume will resolve quickly just because a new chair has taken over.
insights.quote: if you're really admitting that inflation has been above your 2% target for more than 5 years, uh, what are you waiting for?

insights.claim: Yardeni forecasts the Fed will actually raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points in September — a rate HIKE, not a cut — arguing Warsh should have hiked back in July when it would have kept the Fed 'in control of the yield curve,' and that the Fed made policy mistakes cutting rates by 100bp in 2024 and 75bp in 2025 as insurance moves that assumed inflation would keep moderating toward 2%, which it did not.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A call for a September hike is sharply contrarian versus a market generally positioned for cuts; if correct, it implies near-term upside pressure on short rates and a repricing shock for investors positioned for continued easing.
insights.quote: Back in 2024, we argued that there was a mistake to lower the Fed funds rate by 100 basis points. And the bond market agreed with us. Bond yields went up 100 basis points... I think that uh September will be a rate increase.

insights.claim: Warsh reportedly told markets he will focus on the PCE deflator (PCED), not the CPI, as his primary inflation gauge — a specific piece of Fed guidance that matters because the CPI has been running cooler than the PCED (particularly in durable goods), meaning the Fed's preferred underlying inflation read is hotter than the more commonly quoted CPI.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors tracking Fed reaction function should watch core PCED prints specifically rather than CPI headlines, since CPI understates the inflation picture the Fed is actually using to justify hawkish policy.
insights.quote: Not the CPI, but the PCED is what's important. The CPI has actually been running cooler than the PCED, particularly in the durable good side.

insights.claim: Warsh, while campaigning for the Fed chair job with Trump, argued AI-driven productivity gains would lower inflation and justify rate cuts to boost growth (a 'Roaring 2020s' supply-side stance), but after being appointed he pivoted to a hawkish posture on inflation — a notable inconsistency between his pre-appointment rhetoric and his actual policy stance in office.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A documented rhetoric-to-policy flip in a sitting Fed chair is a signal to discount campaign-era policy framing and instead track revealed actions once officials are actually in office.
insights.quote: There was the Worsh who was campaigning interviewing for the job with Trump and he was all supply cider. He said uh AI is going to be a productivity enhancer... But then he got uh anointed as the Fed chair and suddenly he's a hawk on inflation.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent's intervention to support the yen (and reportedly the euro, without consulting the ECB) unsettled the bond market by exposing how dependent the US is on foreign capital flows ('the kindness of strangers') to keep US bond yields in check.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Foreign-exchange intervention by the Treasury is itself a signal of underlying fragility in demand for US Treasuries — a data point for anyone assessing dollar/reserve-currency risk alongside fiscal deficit trends.
insights.quote: we are very dependent on the kindness of strangers and that as a result of that um we uh uh we had to intervene to help the Japanese uh prop up their yen

insights.claim: Bessent's move to double Treasury bond buybacks (from $2bn to $4bn) targeting illiquid off-the-run bonds, followed by a Treasury official publicizing a $1 trillion Treasury General Account 'checking balance' at the Fed as a market backstop, were both dismissed by Yardeni as unimpressive gimmicks — the $1 trillion balance is simply routine cash-management buffer that only gets drawn down during debt-ceiling standoffs, not a discretionary market-support tool.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors should not read Treasury's publicized 'firepower' announcements as new bond-market support tools; the headline $1 trillion figure is accounting normalcy, not incremental buying capacity.
insights.quote: we have a trillion dollars in our uh checking account at the Fed and we'll use that if necessary. But that's kind of a gimmick. It's a joke.

insights.claim: Because Bessent and Druckenmiller both previously ran hedge fund strategies (including a famous short of the British pound under Soros), Yardeni interprets Bessent's true underlying goal as warning off hedge funds currently shorting the 10-year Treasury bond and pushing yields toward 5% — signaling Treasury has a bigger 'toolkit' available if needed, rather than genuinely intervening in currencies for their own sake.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Frames current Treasury actions as a signaling/deterrence game aimed at bond-market speculators rather than substantive policy — useful context for gauging how much further Treasury intervention could realistically escalate if 10-year yields approach 5%.
insights.quote: he's got more in his toolkit if he needs it

insights.claim: Bessent is increasingly financing the federal deficit with short-duration Treasury bills, a strategy he explicitly criticized as 'terrible' when then-Treasury-Secretary Yellen did the same in 2023, but now embraces now that he holds the same position — with stablecoins (legitimized by the Genius Act, which requires them to be backed by liquid securities like T-bills) providing a new structural buyer base for that bill issuance.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Highlights a bipartisan pattern of short-term debt financing being criticized in opposition and embraced in office, while flagging stablecoin-driven demand for T-bills as a genuine new structural buyer that should reduce near-term bond-market stress from heavy bill issuance.
insights.quote: when Yalen did that back in uh 2023, he thought it was a terrible idea. But now that he's in the same same position, he thinks it's probably a very good idea.

themes.theme: Rates: The 'Old Normal' 4-5% Range and Credit Conditions

insights.claim: Yardeni maintains that a 4-5% 10-year Treasury yield range represents a return to the 'old normal' that prevailed before the Great Financial Crisis and the pandemic, reflecting a genuinely strong economy in which the bond market is once again 'allowed to have an opinion,' and argues bond yields have historically been driven far more by inflation and Fed policy than by Treasury supply concerns.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors anchored to the ultra-low-rate 2010s should recalibrate long-run yield expectations toward 4-5% as the durable range rather than treating current levels as an anomaly likely to revert lower.
insights.quote: four to 5% is u the the normal range for the uh for the 10year... back to the old normal where we were before the um great financial crisis through the great virus crisis

insights.claim: Core PCED inflation is running at 3.3% and core PPI for final demand (excluding rent) at a 'hot' 4.4%, while CPI including rent shows a cooler 2.5% — the divergence explains why some observers think inflation is moderating while the Fed's own preferred, broader inflation gauges say otherwise.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete cross-check across CPI, PCED, and PPI shows meaningfully different inflation signals depending on the metric chosen — critical for anyone modeling Fed rate-path scenarios off a single headline number.
insights.quote: if you look at the core PCED it's running 3.3%... there is a core PPI for final demand personal consumption... it does not include rent... so therefore it tends to be higher at 4.4%.

insights.claim: High-yield corporate bond spreads over the 10-year Treasury are very narrow, C&I loan growth is picking up strongly, and Fed officials have stopped referencing the 'neutral rate' as restrictive — implicitly signaling the neutral rate has moved higher because the economy is performing well even at current interest-rate levels.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Narrow credit spreads plus resurgent loan growth argue against an imminent credit-driven slowdown and support the case that current rate levels are not actually restrictive, undercutting the case for near-term rate cuts.
insights.quote: credit spreads are narrow... credit conditions are not restrictive... they're not talking about the neutral rate anymore... implicitly saying the neutral rate has moved higher

themes.theme: The Roaring 2020s: Productivity Boom and Earnings

insights.claim: Yardeni's seven-year productivity cycle chart shows the current productivity boom already exceeding its ~2.5% seven-year average, and he believes it could reach 3-4% (which he acknowledges 'sounds totally crazy and delusional') driven by AI-related technological innovation combined with labor shortages, a stronger combination than in prior productivity booms.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If productivity accelerates to 3-4%, it would materially support the 'Roaring 2020s' bull case of strong growth with contained inflation — a key variable for equity multiple and margin assumptions going forward.
insights.quote: we think it could go to 3 to 4% which sounds totally crazy and delusional but it's that's what uh happens during productivity booms

insights.claim: Unit labor cost growth was just 1.4% year-over-year in Q2 (up from 0.5% in Q1) — evidence, per Yardeni, that productivity gains are already suppressing underlying inflation and supporting an intermediate-to-long-term 'inflation optimist' view even amid near-term stickiness.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Low unit labor cost growth is a leading indicator that could validate a longer-run disinflation case even if headline PCED stays sticky near-term — worth tracking quarterly alongside CPI/PCED.
insights.quote: There's only 1.4% year-over-year in the second quarter. It was 0.5 in the first quarter.

insights.claim: Yardeni notes that Treasury Secretary Bessent is also in the 'Roaring 2020s' camp — his hedge fund wrote a 2024 memo citing this growth framework and bet on a Trump election win translating into pro-growth policy, a trade Yardeni says made the fund good money in 2024, even though tariffs specifically cut against the thesis while deregulation supports it.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Shows the sitting Treasury Secretary's own trading history was built on a pro-growth macro thesis, a useful lens for interpreting why Treasury policy currently favors growth-supportive moves even as some administration policies (tariffs) cut against that same framework.
insights.quote: back uh in early 2024, he wrote a memo for his hedge fund colleagues... at the time he projected that... if Trump got elected president again that's the kind of economic environment he'd like to see happen... they made some pretty good money in their hedge fund in 2024, betting that Trump would win

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings are up almost 50% year-over-year including mark-to-market gains, or about 25% excluding them — an unusually strong reading for mid-cycle expansion, since such acceleration typically only occurs coming out of a recession when both revenues and margins rebound together.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A ~25% ex-mark-to-market earnings growth rate mid-cycle (not post-recession) is historically atypical and supports the bull case that this cycle's earnings power is structurally stronger than prior expansions, not just a rebound effect.
insights.quote: This is S&P 500 earnings uh up almost 50% on a year-over-year basis. Take out the marktomarket gains and you get a gain of about 25%.

insights.claim: Yardeni's S&P 500 year-end price target of roughly 8,400 is derived mechanically: the 2027 consensus EPS estimate (already near $412/share, with his target of $415) multiplied by a 20.24x forward P/E, with forward earnings defined as a time-weighted average of current-year and next-year estimates that converges toward the 2027 figure.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives investors the exact mechanical formula (EPS estimate x forward multiple) behind Yardeni's headline S&P 500 target, letting them stress-test it against their own EPS or multiple assumptions.
insights.quote: $415 a share... where forward earnings will get to. and then multiply it by 20.24. Uh that's the exact PE. That'll get you to... 8,400

insights.claim: Earnings strength is broadening beyond mega-cap technology into small-cap and mid-cap stocks as well, according to Yardeni's read of the current earnings season.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Broadening earnings growth beyond large-cap tech supports a more resilient, less concentration-dependent equity bull case, relevant for rotation strategies into small/mid-cap exposure.
insights.quote: the uh earnings uh picture continues to broaden out. Uh small cap, midcap, large caps, all doing really well.

insights.claim: Yardeni reiterates a $5,000 year-end gold price target (explicitly caveating it 'doesn't come with a money-back guarantee'), viewing rising short-term interest rates as bearish for gold in the near term but central banks as the ultimate backstop buyers who would view any dip as a buying opportunity, and doubts gold retests its prior $4,000 level even though it currently sits slightly below its 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable $5,000 year-end gold target with an explicit mechanism (central bank buying as the floor, rate hikes as the near-term headwind) gives investors a specific level and rationale to track against.
insights.quote: we're still using 5,000 by the end of the year. Um doesn't come with a money back guarantee, by the way.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects a possible equity market stall or selloff between September and the midterms, viewing that as a likely buying opportunity ahead of a fourth-quarter rally, following the seasonal pattern where market lows are typically made in October before earnings-driven strength resumes.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives a specific tactical roadmap — expect September weakness, buy the dip, and expect Q4 strength into the 8,400 target — useful for investors weighing near-term entry timing.
insights.quote: a September stall or sell a sell selloff would probably be a buying opportunity and then uh October is when you typically make the lows uh in a September October sell-off and then uh we could uh move higher

insights.claim: Yardeni explicitly declines to offer a firm view yet on tokenization and stablecoins despite them being a major topic at the Jackson Hole symposium, saying his team is still reviewing the relevant papers and speeches before forming an informed opinion, but flags it broadly as an important emerging fintech/blockchain theme.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Signals tokenization/stablecoin infrastructure is moving onto mainstream macro strategists' radar as a theme worth monitoring, even before a firm investment view has been formed.
insights.quote: it's not just tokenization, it's also uh stable coins and you know using uh blockchain uh more in the financial system... it's it's fintech.
